name: English Lavender
description: Famous for its fragrant purple blooms, Lavender is prized for its soothing essential oils, peaceful fragrance, and medicinal properties that promote restful sleep and reduce stress.

growingConditions.watering: Low water requirement once established; drought tolerant

uses: Aromatherapy for stress reduction and sleep improvement
Infused in herbal teas, lemonade, and delicate pastries
Dried sachets for closet fresheners and essential oil extraction
Attracts beneficial pollinators like bees and butterflies

video.title: Growing and caring for lavender plants

uses: Aromatherapy and pillow sachets to encourage relaxation and restful sleep
Tea or diluted oil traditionally used for stress and nervous tension
Diluted oil applied to minor burns, insect bites and headaches in folk practice
benefits: Calming scent shown in small studies to reduce feelings of anxiety
Contains linalool and linalyl acetate, aromatic compounds linked to relaxation
Mild antiseptic properties used for skin care
medicinal.caution: Never swallow lavender essential oil, and always dilute it before it touches the skin, as it can cause irritation in some people.

taste: Floral and slightly sweet, with a herbal, piney edge. A little goes a long way.
sideEffects: Lavender essential oil must never be swallowed
Undiluted oil can irritate the skin
Can cause drowsiness, so be careful when driving after strong lavender products

safety.allergy: Lavender oil can cause skin rashes in some people. Test a diluted drop on the inner arm first, and stop using it if the skin itches or turns red.
safety.pregnancy: Cooking amounts and gentle scent are generally fine, but avoid essential oil and medicinal doses unless a doctor agrees.
safety.pets: Lavender can upset the stomach of cats and dogs, and the oil can be harmful, so keep both out of reach.
safety.medications: Lavender may add to the sleepy effect of sedatives and sleeping tablets. Ask your doctor if you take them.

temperature: Loves hot, dry summers. English lavender copes with winter cold of around -15 °C if the soil stays dry, but it hates wet winter roots.
harvest: Cut the flower stems when about half of the buds on a spike have opened, in the morning after the dew has dried. Cut above the leaves and leave some green growth. Do not cut into old bare wood, because it will not regrow.
storage: Tie small bunches and hang them upside down in a dark, airy place for two to four weeks. When crisp, rub the buds off and keep them in an airtight jar away from light for up to a year.
dailyLife: Put a dried sachet near the pillow for a calming bedtime scent
Add a few buds to shortbread, honey or sugar
Brew a small pinch of buds as a relaxing tea
Hang a bunch in a wardrobe to freshen clothes
tips: Give it plenty of sun and very good drainage
Trim lightly after flowering, but never into old wood
Poor, stony soil gives the strongest scent

origin.details: English lavender comes from the mountains of the western Mediterranean. The fields of southern France are famous for it.
